short: The first tank ever used in battle, on the Somme in September 1916.
full:
Forty-nine Mark I tanks were sent to the Somme for the attack at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916; thirty-two reached their start points and about nine kept pace with the infantry. They came in two forms: male tanks with two 6-pounder guns in side sponsons, and female tanks armed only with machine guns. A crew of eight worked in heat and fumes at a top speed of under four miles per hour, steering with the help of a wheeled tail.

The attack took Flers and some of the deepest ground gained on the Somme, and Haig was criticised for spending the surprise on a small, unreliable batch. He ordered a thousand more. Mark Is fought again in 1917, including eight sent to Palestine for the Second Battle of Gaza in April, the first use of tanks in desert conditions. Survivors were then converted to supply and wireless carriers, while the rhomboid hull shape ran on through the Mark IV to the Mark VIII.
